paper.citation: Meng YA, Yu Y, Cupples LA, Farrer LA, Lunetta KL. Performance of random forest when SNPs are in linkage disequilibrium. BMC Bioinformatics 10:78 (2009)

exceptions.evidence: The model gives 5.2266 (5.2255 with the allele frequency that makes lambda_s = 9 exactly, 0.12503); both round to 5.23, not the printed 5.22 (output/table1.json).
As for het: the model has equal het and hom GRRs here (q1 = q2), 5.2266.

items.label: Table 5, the 13 LD models

cause.summary: A design table: it defines the LD models the simulation uses (rfld.LD_MODELS).

items.label: Fig. 1, mean IM of the risk SNPs (40 bars)

assumptions.what: Published bar heights, error bars and curve points read off the PMC figure JPEGs (600 px wide) through each axis's tick marks
assumptions.sensitivity: Tick fits within 0.4 px; one pixel is 0.006 IM in Fig. 1, 0.003 in Fig. 2 and about 0.005 in Figs 3-6, and is added to every tolerance. Curve points where another curve hides the series are not read.

assumptions.what: IM is printed as 100 x the mean decrease in accuracy over trees, as Random Forests 5.1 writes it; Eq. 1 of the paper has a factor 2/T
assumptions.sensitivity: With the factor 2 every IM doubles: our no-LD RF0:IM0 would be 1.31 against the published 0.64, outside the tolerance (0.13). Without it, 0.65.

assumptions.what: RF1 threshold R = 0.5 (the paper does not give it)
assumptions.sensitivity: LD SNPs are perfect proxies (r2 = 1) and noise SNPs correlate by chance up to r2 of about 0.03-0.05, so every R from about 0.05 to just below 1 gives the same forests. R = 0.02 also drops chance-correlated noise SNPs; it is in summary.json as RF1(R=0.02) and lowers the risk SNPs' IM0 (see the RF1 cause of Fig. 1).

assumptions.what: The 13 LD models of a replicate are built on the same n0 data set (incremental), for H4M4 as for the other models
assumptions.sensitivity: The paper says it built the other models incrementally; for H4M4 its wording is ambiguous, and its Figs 1-2 n series fall too smoothly for independent data sets. Each LD model on its own data (snp_independent in summary.json) changes no conclusion: Fig. 1 also comes back 40 of 40.

assumptions.what: Cases are the first 250 affected and controls the first 250 unaffected people drawn from the population model (Lunetta et al. 2004 do not say how the samples were drawn)
assumptions.sensitivity: Not tested; drawing controls from the whole population would add about 10% affected people to the controls of H4M4 (K = 0.098).

items.label: Text: the original IM of the risk SNPs falls as LD.rSNPs are added, under all models
Text: RF0:IM0 and RF1:IM0 differ very little for a fixed number of LD.rSNPs (Fig. 1)
Text: RF0:IM1 is steadier than RF1:IM1 as LD.rSNPs are added, under all models
Text: RF1:IM1 is inflated as LD.rSNPs are added
Main claim: the revised IM with the original RF (RF0:IM1) is the most stable under LD
Discussion: SNPs in LD with noise SNPs have little effect (data not shown)
Text: in Fig. 2, the revised RF with the original IM (RF1:IM0) is the most stable
Discussion: in Fig. 2, RF1:IM1 performs best and improves with more LD.rSNPs
Text: with LD.rSNPs the top-X share is lower for small X (8) and higher for X >= 20 (30)
Text: for a fixed number of LD.rSNPs, RF0 beats RF1 in Fig. 3
Text: mean IM rHAP > PRED.rHAP > rSNP in general, the gap closing as r2 rises (Fig. 4)
Text: the IM of the risk SNPs rises with LD between them (Fig. 4)
Text: the share above the noise rises with LD between the risk SNPs (Fig. 5)
Discussion: predicted haplotypes perform between risk SNPs and true haplotypes (Fig. 5)
Text: 7 of the 17 top SNPs would be missed by single-SNP tests (TGen data)

cause.summary: Needs the TGen genotypes (Tables 2-4). The count itself follows from Table 4 (text.arithmetic): 7 of 17.
